   155→| 3    | POST /ipns/publish-batch        | 0.11s       | DB upsert for file IPNS record   |
   156→| 4    | POST /ipfs/upload (folder meta) | **1.73s**   | Pin updated folder metadata      |
   157→| 5    | POST /ipns/publish              | 0.14s       | DB upsert for folder IPNS record |

   162→
   163→| Metric                          | Count   | Mean  | Notes                                               |
   164→| ------------------------------- | ------- | ----- | --------------------------------------------------- |
   165→| IPFS Pin (Kubo `pin add`)       | 172,387 | 1.56s | ~95% of upload endpoint time                        |
   166→| HTTP POST /ipfs/upload          | 172,387 | 1.64s | Pin + quota check + DB write                        |
   167→| IPNS Publish (DB upsert)        | 122,892 | 127ms | Fast — just a database write                        |
   168→| IPNS Publish Batch (DB upsert)  | 24,717  | 92ms  | Similar to single publish                           |
   169→| IPNS Publish (409 conflict)     | 1       | 4ms   | Expected at high concurrency (seq number collision) |
   170→| Async DHT propagation (success) | 147,285 | 838ms | Fire-and-forget, does not block client              |
   171→| Async DHT propagation (error)   | 324     | 17.2s | 0.22% error rate, does not affect client responses  |
   172→
   173→### Bottleneck analysis
   174→
   175→**Kubo IPFS pinning is the dominant bottleneck**, consuming ~95% of the upload endpoint latency. Each `uploadFile` requires 3 sequential pin operations (ciphertext, file metadata, folder metadata), totaling ~5s server-side at mean.
   176→
   177→IPNS publishing is negligible in the request path (DB upsert only, ~100-140ms). DHT propagation happens asynchronously and does not block the client.
   178→
   179→**Levers for improving upload performance:**
   180→
   181→- **Concurrent pins**: The 3 pin calls per upload are currently sequential. Pins 1+2 (ciphertext + file metadata) could be parallelized since they're independent.
   182→- **Kubo tuning**: Pin performance degrades under concurrent load — likely contention on Kubo's datastore. Investigate Kubo's `--pin-workers` setting or a faster datastore backend.
   183→- **Pin batching**: Multiple small metadata pins could potentially be coalesced.
   184→
   185→## Comparison Targets
   186→
   187→Phase 22 (Performance Baselines Completion) should:
   188→
   189→- Re-capture server-side Prometheus histograms for direct comparison with Phase 18 internal timings
   190→- Add client-side instrumentation for real user latency measurement
   191→- Document capacity limits and scaling recommendations
   192→- Performance regression threshold: >20% p95 increase requires investigation

# Performance Baselines - Phase 19 (Someguy IPNS Sidecar)

## Capture Information

| Field            | Value                                                              |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Capture Date** | 2026-03-23                                                         |
| **Environment**  | Staging (api-staging.cipherbox.cc) + Local (192.168.133.114)       |
| **Kubo Version** | v0.40.0                                                            |
| **Someguy**      | v0.11.1 (ghcr.io/ipfs/someguy)                                     |
| **API Image**    | cipher-box-v0.26.5                                                 |
| **VPS**          | Hostinger KVM2, 4 vCPU, 8GB RAM                                    |
| **Test Suite**   | SDK E2E (83 tests) + Load tests (vitest, custom metrics collector) |
| **DHT Warm-up**  | ~8 hours on staging, ~10 minutes on local                          |

## Someguy Configuration

| Setting                     | Previous (broken, PR #284) | Fixed (PR #325)              |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| libp2p port 4004            | Not exposed                | Exposed (TCP + UDP)          |
| DHT mode                    | `standard`                 | `accelerated`                |
| Connection limits           | 50/300                     | 100/3000 (defaults)          |
| `SOMEGUY_LIBP2P_MAX_MEMORY` | 512MB                      | 1073741824 (1GB)             |
| Container memory            | 768MB                      | 2GB                          |
| Container CPU               | 0.5                        | 1.0                          |
| Healthcheck start period    | 30s                        | 60s                          |
| Fallback URL                | None                       | `https://delegated-ipfs.dev` |

Root cause of Phase 19's initial failure: no libp2p port exposed meant DHT couldn't receive inbound connections, `standard` mode skipped accelerated FullRT client, and tight resource limits triggered libp2p Resource Manager errors.

## SDK E2E Results (83 tests)

| Environment       | Passed | Failed | Skipped |
| ----------------- | ------ | ------ | ------- |
| Local (someguy)   | 83     | 0      | 0       |
| Staging (someguy) | 83     | 0      | 0       |

All 83 tests pass with zero errors on both environments.

## Load Test: IPNS Publish Storm (5 clients × 50 cycles = 750 ops)

### Cross-environment comparison

| Metric           | Staging (someguy, warm DHT) | Local (delegated-ipfs.dev) | Local (someguy, cold DHT) |
| ---------------- | --------------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| Duration         | **49.1s**                   | 69.7s                      | 89.3s                     |
| Throughput       | **15.28 ops/s**             | 10.75 ops/s                | 8.39 ops/s                |
| Errors           | **0**                       | **0**                      | **0**                     |
| createFolder p50 | **468ms**                   | 606ms                      | 728ms                     |
| createFolder p95 | **848ms**                   | 1.22s                      | 1.07s                     |
| createFolder p99 | **1.0s**                    | 1.62s                      | 1.27s                     |
| deleteItem p50   | **246ms**                   | 395ms                      | 469ms                     |
| deleteItem p95   | **476ms**                   | 690ms                      | 795ms                     |
| renameItem p50   | **182ms**                   | 305ms                      | 520ms                     |
| renameItem p95   | **377ms**                   | 704ms                      | 1.06s                     |

### Comparison vs Phase 18 baselines

| Metric              | Phase 18 (Kubo direct, 5 clients) | Phase 19 staging (someguy, 5 clients) | Change         |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | -------------- |
| Throughput          | 1.25 ops/sec                      | **15.28 ops/sec**                     | **+12.2x**     |
| Error rate          | 4.6% (18/395)                     | **0%** (0/750)                        | **Eliminated** |
| Total ops attempted | 395                               | 750                                   | +90% more ops  |
| Total ops succeeded | 377                               | 750                                   | +99%           |

Note: Phase 18 measured via Playwright browser automation (higher overhead per op), Phase 19 via SDK direct calls. The measurement difference accounts for some of the throughput gap, but the zero error rate is the significant improvement — Phase 18 had 18 timeouts under identical concurrency.

## Load Test: Mixed Workload (5 clients × 45 mixed ops)

| Metric           | Staging (someguy) | Local (delegated-ipfs.dev) | Local (someguy, cold DHT) |
| ---------------- | ----------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| Duration         | **23.6s**         | 40.4s                      | 58.9s                     |
| Throughput       | **9.32 ops/s**    | 5.50 ops/s                 | 3.68 ops/s                |
| Errors           | **0**             | **0**                      | **0**                     |
| createFolder p50 | **511ms**         | 840ms                      | 1.4s                      |
| deleteItem p50   | **215ms**         | 338ms                      | 539ms                     |
| moveItem p50     | **442ms**         | 659ms                      | 1.2s                      |
| renameItem p50   | **195ms**         | 390ms                      | 623ms                     |
| uploadFile p50   | **613ms**         | 1.1s                       | 1.5s                      |
| Data transferred | 2.5MB             | 2.9MB                      | 2.6MB                     |

## Key Observations

1. **DHT warm-up matters significantly**: Staging someguy (8h uptime) is ~2x faster than local someguy (10min uptime). The accelerated DHT routing table fills over time, improving lookup speed.

2. **Someguy with warm DHT beats delegated-ipfs.dev**: 42% higher throughput and ~40-50% lower median latency across all operations. The public fleet advantage disappears once the local sidecar's DHT is populated.

3. **Zero errors across all test runs**: Both SDK E2E (83 tests) and load tests (750+ ops) complete with zero failures, compared to Phase 18's 4.6% error rate.

4. **DB-first resolve architecture unchanged**: IPNS resolution still goes through the database as primary source of truth. Someguy's value is in reliable DHT publishing for TEE republishing and the standalone recovery tool, not in replacing DB resolves.

5. **Fallback to delegated-ipfs.dev**: Configured via `DELEGATED_ROUTING_FALLBACK_URL`. Prometheus counter `cipherbox_delegated_routing_fallbacks_total` tracks when primary (someguy) fails and fallback is used.

## Prometheus Metrics Available

New metrics added in this phase for ongoing monitoring:

| Metric                                        | Labels                      | Purpose                                       |
| --------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `cipherbox_delegated_routing_requests_total`  | operation, backend, outcome | Every routing request tagged primary/fallback |
| `cipherbox_delegated_routing_fallbacks_total` | operation                   | Count of primary→fallback triggers            |
| `cipherbox_ipns_publish_duration_seconds`     | outcome                     | Delegated routing publish latency             |
| `cipherbox_ipns_resolve_duration_seconds`     | source, outcome             | End-to-end resolve latency                    |

## Extended Load Test: Mixed Workload Scaling (10–200 clients)

Captured 2026-03-23 via GitHub Actions against staging. Mixed Workload scenario: weighted mix of createFolder, uploadFile, moveItem, deleteItem, renameItem.

### Throughput scaling

| Clients | Total Ops | Errors | Throughput  | Duration | Data   |

| 5       | 220       | 0      | 9.32 ops/s  | 23.6s    | 2.5MB  |
| 10      | 434       | 0      | 4.49 ops/s  | 96.6s    | 5.2MB  |
| 20      | 856       | 0      | 8.42 ops/s  | 101.7s   | 9.6MB  |
| 30      | 1,299     | 0      | 12.14 ops/s | 107.0s   | 14.4MB |
| 50      | 2,171     | 0      | 22.86 ops/s | 95.0s    | 23.1MB |
| 75      | 3,267     | 0      | 23.60 ops/s | 138.4s   | 36.2MB |
| 100     | 4,355     | 0      | 24.05 ops/s | 181.1s   | 49.4MB |
| 200     | 8,734     | 4      | 28.50 ops/s | 306.5s   | 97.3MB |

Note: The 5-client baseline was run separately (different network path). The 10–200 client runs are directly comparable.

### Latency by operation (p50 / p95 / p99)

| ------------ | ------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------- | -------------------- |
| createFolder | 1.9s / 3.1s / 4.4s  | 2.0s / 3.3s / 3.6s  | 2.4s / 3.5s / 4.2s  | 2.0s / 3.3s / 4.9s  | 2.9s / 4.8s / 7.4s | 3.7s / 6.5s / 8.0s  | 6.2s / 10.3s / 17.8s |
| uploadFile   | 2.6s / 3.9s / 4.7s  | 2.8s / 4.4s / 4.8s  | 3.0s / 4.5s / 5.2s  | 2.7s / 4.3s / 5.4s  | 3.9s / 6.4s / 9.1s | 5.1s / 7.8s / 11.6s | 8.8s / 13.5s / 21.0s |
| moveItem     | 1.9s / 2.6s / 3.4s  | 1.9s / 2.9s / 3.4s  | 2.3s / 3.1s / 3.7s  | 1.8s / 2.9s / 3.2s  | 2.7s / 4.4s / 5.1s | 3.5s / 5.6s / 6.7s  | 6.1s / 9.0s / 10.4s  |
| deleteItem   | 815ms / 1.8s / 2.4s | 881ms / 1.8s / 2.0s | 929ms / 1.8s / 2.1s | 890ms / 1.9s / 2.4s | 1.4s / 2.4s / 2.7s | 1.9s / 3.2s / 4.3s  | 3.0s / 4.9s / 5.9s   |

### Scaling observations

1. **Throughput plateaus at ~23-28 ops/s**: From 50→200 clients, throughput only grows from 22.86→28.50 ops/s. The staging VPS (4 vCPU, 8GB) is saturated — additional clients primarily increase latency.
2. **The knee is at ~50 clients**: Throughput jumps from 12.14 (30 clients) to 22.86 (50 clients), then flattens. Kubo's pin concurrency maxes out around 50 parallel operations.
3. **First errors at 200 clients**: 4 errors across 8,734 ops (0.05% error rate). 1 each in createFolder, moveItem, renameItem, uploadFile. Also 1 IPNS publish 409 conflict (expected concurrent sequence number collision). Error-free operation up to 100 clients.
4. **uploadFile p99 reaches 21s at 200 clients**: p50 grows from 2.6s (10 clients) to 8.8s (200 clients). p99 goes from 4.7s to 21.0s — approaching typical HTTP timeout thresholds.
5. **Kubo pin mean stays flat (~1.6s)**: Server-side pin latency doesn't degrade much with concurrency. The client-side latency increase is primarily queuing — more clients waiting for their turn.
6. **Metadata-only operations degrade gracefully**: deleteItem/renameItem p50 grows from ~750ms (10 clients) to ~3.0s (200 clients).

## Upload Flow Latency Breakdown (Prometheus Server-Side)

Captured from staging `/metrics` endpoint after all load test runs (10–200 clients). Cumulative histograms.

### Where uploadFile time goes

A single SDK `uploadFile` call makes 5 sequential API calls:

| Step | API Call                        | Server Mean | Role                             |
| ---- | ------------------------------- | ----------- | -------------------------------- |
| 1    | POST /ipfs/upload (ciphertext)  | **1.73s**   | Pin encrypted file to Kubo       |
| 2    | POST /ipfs/upload (metadata)    | **1.73s**   | Pin encrypted file metadata      |
| 3    | POST /ipns/publish-batch        | 0.11s       | DB upsert for file IPNS record   |
| 4    | POST /ipfs/upload (folder meta) | **1.73s**   | Pin updated folder metadata      |
| 5    | POST /ipns/publish              | 0.14s       | DB upsert for folder IPNS record |

**Total server-side: ~5.4s** — aligns with the 5.1s p50 client-side at 100 clients.

### Internal operation timing

| Metric                          | Count   | Mean  | Notes                                               |
| ------------------------------- | ------- | ----- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| IPFS Pin (Kubo `pin add`)       | 172,387 | 1.56s | ~95% of upload endpoint time                        |
| HTTP POST /ipfs/upload          | 172,387 | 1.64s | Pin + quota check + DB write                        |
| IPNS Publish (DB upsert)        | 122,892 | 127ms | Fast — just a database write                        |
| IPNS Publish Batch (DB upsert)  | 24,717  | 92ms  | Similar to single publish                           |
| IPNS Publish (409 conflict)     | 1       | 4ms   | Expected at high concurrency (seq number collision) |
| Async DHT propagation (success) | 147,285 | 838ms | Fire-and-forget, does not block client              |
| Async DHT propagation (error)   | 324     | 17.2s | 0.22% error rate, does not affect client responses  |

### Bottleneck analysis

**Kubo IPFS pinning is the dominant bottleneck**, consuming ~95% of the upload endpoint latency. Each `uploadFile` requires 3 sequential pin operations (ciphertext, file metadata, folder metadata), totaling ~5s server-side at mean.

IPNS publishing is negligible in the request path (DB upsert only, ~100-140ms). DHT propagation happens asynchronously and does not block the client.

**Levers for improving upload performance:**

- **Concurrent pins**: The 3 pin calls per upload are currently sequential. Pins 1+2 (ciphertext + file metadata) could be parallelized since they're independent.
- **Kubo tuning**: Pin performance degrades under concurrent load — likely contention on Kubo's datastore. Investigate Kubo's `--pin-workers` setting or a faster datastore backend.
- **Pin batching**: Multiple small metadata pins could potentially be coalesced.

## Comparison Targets

Phase 22 (Performance Baselines Completion) should:

- Re-capture server-side Prometheus histograms for direct comparison with Phase 18 internal timings
- Add client-side instrumentation for real user latency measurement
- Document capacity limits and scaling recommendations
- Performance regression threshold: >20% p95 increase requires investigation

# Roadmap: CipherBox Milestone 4 -- Encrypted Productivity Suite

## Overview

Milestone 4 transforms CipherBox from an encrypted file locker into an encrypted productivity platform. Five phases follow the natural dependency chain: billing infrastructure (gates tier-based access), team accounts (enables shared vaults with ECIES-wrapped Per-Team Keys), document editors (TipTap rich text + Univer spreadsheets with decrypt-edit-encrypt pipeline), document signing (ECDSA attestation using existing Web3Auth keys), and AWS Nitro TEE (fallback republisher moved from M2). Real-time collaboration is explicitly deferred to M5+; M4 delivers single-user editing with advisory locking for team documents.

## Phases

**Phase Numbering:**

- Continues from M3 (Phases 18-22). M4 starts at Phase 23.
- Integer phases (23, 24, 25, 26, 27): Planned milestone work
- Decimal phases (e.g., 24.1): Urgent insertions (marked with INSERTED)

Decimal phases appear between their surrounding integers in numeric order.

- [ ] **Phase 23: Billing Infrastructure** - Stripe subscriptions, NOWPayments crypto billing, tier enforcement, and webhook-driven provisioning
- [ ] **Phase 24: Team Accounts** - Team CRUD, ECIES-wrapped Per-Team Key hierarchy, CASL role-based permissions, team vault initialization
- [ ] **Phase 25: Document Editors** - TipTap rich text and Univer spreadsheet editors with decrypt-edit-encrypt pipeline, autosave queue, advisory locking
- [ ] **Phase 26: Document Signing** - ECDSA signing/verification with Web3Auth keys, visual signature capture, multi-party workflows, signed PDF export
- [ ] **Phase 27: AWS Nitro TEE** - Nitro enclave as fallback TEE provider for IPNS republishing (moved from M2)

## Phase Details

### Phase 23: Billing Infrastructure

**Goal**: Users can subscribe to paid plans and the system enforces storage and feature limits by tier
**Depends on**: Phase 22 (Milestone 3 complete)
**Requirements**: BILL-01, BILL-02, BILL-03, BILL-04, BILL-05, BILL-06, BILL-07, BILL-08
**Research flag**: Standard patterns -- Stripe integration is well-documented with mature NestJS modules. NOWPayments REST API is straightforward. Skip `/gsd:research-phase`.
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

1. User can select a plan (Free/Pro/Team), complete Stripe Checkout, and see their subscription activated within seconds of payment
2. User can open Stripe Customer Portal from settings to upgrade, downgrade, or cancel their subscription without contacting support
3. Pro user uploading files beyond the free 500 MiB limit succeeds up to 50 GiB; free user is blocked at 500 MiB with an upgrade prompt
4. User can pay with cryptocurrency (BTC, ETH, USDC) via NOWPayments; subscription activates after blockchain confirmation
5. When a user's payment fails, they retain access for a grace period and receive notification; access downgrades only after grace period expires

**Plans**: TBD

### Phase 24: Team Accounts

**Goal**: Users can create teams with shared encrypted vaults where team members access shared content through a zero-knowledge key hierarchy
**Depends on**: Phase 23 (billing tier enforcement for team member limits)
**Requirements**: TEAM-01, TEAM-02, TEAM-03, TEAM-04, TEAM-05, TEAM-06, TEAM-07, TEAM-08, TEAM-09
**Research flag**: NEEDS `/gsd:research-phase` -- PTK rotation on member removal is the most complex protocol in M4. ECIES re-wrapping correctness with key epochs must be validated. IPNS record size under team metadata growth (N members x M wrapped keys) needs measurement.
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

1. User can create a team, and the team vault is initialized with a team-scoped IPNS keypair and root folder key (all encrypted with the Per-Team Key, never plaintext on server)
2. Owner can invite a member by email or public key; the PTK is ECIES-wrapped to the invitee's publicKey; invitee can accept and immediately browse team files
3. User can switch between personal vault and team vaults in the sidebar; folder navigation within a team vault works identically to the personal vault
4. Owner can remove a member, which triggers PTK rotation -- the removed member can no longer decrypt newly encrypted team content
5. Team of 25 members on a Team tier operates without hitting member limits; free/pro users attempting to create teams are prompted to upgrade

**Plans**: TBD

### Phase 25: Document Editors

**Goal**: Users can create and edit rich text documents and spreadsheets directly in the browser with all content encrypted at rest on IPFS
**Depends on**: Phase 24 (team vaults for shared document editing context and advisory locking)
**Requirements**: EDIT-01, EDIT-02, EDIT-03, EDIT-04, EDIT-05, EDIT-06, EDIT-07, EDIT-08, EDIT-09
**Research flag**: NEEDS `/gsd:research-phase` -- TipTap 3.x + Univer integration specifics, bundle size impact, autosave pipeline performance with IPFS/IPNS latency. A proof-of-concept of the decrypt-edit-encrypt pipeline should be built early in planning.
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

1. User can create a new document, type and format text (bold, italic, headings, lists, links, tables), and the content is encrypted and persisted to IPFS on save
2. User can reopen a previously saved document and see their content exactly as they left it (round-trip through encrypt/decrypt preserves formatting)
3. User can create and edit a spreadsheet with formulas, formatting, and multiple sheets; spreadsheet state is encrypted and persisted identically to documents
4. Autosave fires after 60 seconds of inactivity; a dirty indicator shows unsaved changes; closing the tab with unsaved changes triggers a warning
5. When a team member opens a team document for editing, other team members see an advisory lock indicator and can choose read-only view or force-edit

**Plans**: TBD

### Phase 26: Document Signing

**Goal**: Users can cryptographically sign documents with their Web3Auth keys and any authorized party can verify the signature
**Depends on**: Phase 25 (documents exist to be signed; editor infrastructure provides the document viewing context)
**Requirements**: SIGN-01, SIGN-02, SIGN-03, SIGN-04, SIGN-05, SIGN-06
**Research flag**: Standard patterns -- uses existing ECDSA primitives (secp256k1 via Web3Auth + Web Crypto API). Straightforward implementation. Skip `/gsd:research-phase`.
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

1. User can sign any document or file, producing an ECDSA signature over the SHA-256 content hash; signature metadata is stored in encrypted folder metadata
2. Any user with folder access can verify a signature is valid for the given document content and signer's publicKey
3. User can draw or type a visual signature that is displayed alongside the cryptographic signature status in the file browser
4. User can request signatures from other CipherBox users; the document shows signature status (pending/partial/complete) and lists who has and has not signed
5. User can export a signed document as a PDF with the digital signature embedded (client-side via LibPDF)

**Plans**: TBD

### Phase 27: AWS Nitro TEE

**Goal**: IPNS republishing has a fallback TEE provider for high availability (moved from M2 — Phala Cloud mock still in use on staging)
**Depends on**: Phase 12 (can run in parallel with Phases 23-26)
**Requirements**: TEE-06
**Research flag**: NEEDS `/gsd:research-phase` -- Rust enclave binary, vsock communication, KMS attestation are entirely new technology for this project.
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

1. AWS Nitro enclave can receive ECIES-encrypted IPNS keys, decrypt in hardware, sign IPNS records, and zero memory
2. Backend routes republish jobs to Nitro when Phala Cloud is unavailable, with automatic failover and failback

**Plans**: TBD

| 26. Document Signing       | M4        | 0/TBD          | Not started | -         |
| 27. AWS Nitro TEE          | M4        | 0/TBD          | Not started | -         |

---

# Roadmap: CipherBox v1.1 IPFS Infrastructure

## Overview

CipherBox v1.1 transforms the platform from "IPFS as a storage backend with database fallbacks" to "IPFS-native with the database serving only auth." The milestone establishes performance baselines before making changes, replaces the unreliable delegated-ipfs.dev dependency with self-hosted IPNS resolution, migrates rootFolderKey to an IPFS vault blob (achieving true zero-knowledge server), adds BYO-IPFS node support for data sovereignty, and completes performance baselines with client-side instrumentation and load testing after all features are stable.

## Milestones

- **v0.1 Staging MVP** - Phases 1-10 (shipped 2026-02-11)
- **v1.0 Production** - Phases 11-17.1 (shipped 2026-03-05)
- **v1.1 IPFS Infrastructure** - Phases 18-22 (in progress)

## Phases

**Phase Numbering:**

- Integer phases (1, 2, 3): Planned milestone work
- Decimal phases (2.1, 2.2): Urgent insertions (marked with INSERTED)

Decimal phases appear between their surrounding integers in numeric order.

- [x] **Phase 18: Performance Instrumentation** - Server-side Prometheus histograms and Kubo metrics scraping to establish baselines before any architectural changes (completed 2026-03-07)
- [x] **Phase 19: IPNS Resolution Improvement** - Replace delegated-ipfs.dev with self-hosted Someguy sidecar for reliable IPNS routing, add latency histograms for resolve/publish operations (completed 2026-03-07)
- [ ] **Phase 20: Vault Migration** - Move rootFolderKey to IPFS vault blob v2 format, making the server store zero crypto material
- [ ] **Phase 21: BYO-IPFS Node Support** - User-configurable IPFS pinning endpoint with dual-pin strategy, Settings UI, and connection testing
- [ ] **Phase 22: Performance Baselines Completion** - Client-side timing instrumentation, end-to-end journey timing, k6 load testing, and capacity documentation

## Phase Details

### Phase 18: Performance Instrumentation

**Goal**: Operators can observe IPFS/IPNS latency and API performance in Prometheus/Grafana before any architectural changes are made
**Depends on**: Nothing (first phase of milestone)
**Requirements**: PERF-01, PERF-02, PERF-03, PERF-04
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

1. Prometheus exposes duration histograms for IPNS resolve, IPNS publish, IPFS pin, and IPFS cat operations with per-operation labels
2. API endpoint response times are captured at p50/p95/p99 for all critical routes (auth, IPNS resolve/publish, file upload/download, folder CRUD)
3. Kubo node health metrics (peer count, bandwidth, datastore size) are visible in Prometheus via scraped Kubo endpoint
4. TEE republish batch duration histogram captures per-batch timing with success/failure labels

**Plans:** 2/2 plans complete

Plans:

- [x] 18-01-PLAN.md -- Add IPFS/IPNS + TEE duration histograms to MetricsService and instrument service/controller timing
- [x] 18-02-PLAN.md -- Add Kubo scrape to Alloy, extend Grafana dashboard, create baseline benchmark script

### Phase 19: IPNS Resolution Improvement

**Goal**: Users experience reliable, fast IPNS resolution without dependency on external delegated-ipfs.dev service
**Depends on**: Phase 18 (baselines must exist to measure improvement)
**Requirements**: IPNS-01, IPNS-02, IPNS-03, IPNS-04
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

1. Self-hosted Someguy is deployed alongside Kubo and serves as the IPNS routing provider, with delegated-ipfs.dev fully removed from the resolution path
2. IPNS resolution completes within 2 seconds in the normal case (DB-first with async DHT verification) and degrades gracefully to DB-only when DHT is slow
3. The standalone recovery tool resolves IPNS records via self-hosted Someguy without depending on the CipherBox API or delegated-ipfs.dev
4. No user-visible errors or stale metadata when the DHT is temporarily unreachable (DB fallback serves correct data)
   **Plans**: 2 plans

Plans:

- [x] 19-01-PLAN.md -- Deploy Someguy Docker sidecar, update routing URL in deploy workflow and .env.example
- [x] 19-02-PLAN.md -- Add IPNS resolve/publish latency histograms and instrument IpnsService with timing

### Phase 19.1: Extract core crypto SDK as shared package (INSERTED)

**Goal:** Web app's crypto and file operation logic is extracted into a five-package layered SDK architecture (@cipherbox/crypto, @cipherbox/core, @cipherbox/api-client, @cipherbox/sdk-core, @cipherbox/sdk) enabling load testing, integration testing, and future CLI usage without a browser context
**Requirements**: SDK-01, SDK-02, SDK-03, SDK-04, SDK-05, SDK-06, SDK-07, SDK-08, SDK-09, SDK-10, SDK-11
**Depends on:** Phase 19
**Plans:** 6/6 plans complete

Plans:

- [ ] 19.1-01-PLAN.md -- Split crypto into crypto + core packages with transitional re-exports
- [ ] 19.1-02-PLAN.md -- Expand api-client package with orval generation and configurable instance
- [ ] 19.1-03-PLAN.md -- Create sdk-core with stateless folder/file/IPFS/IPNS operations
- [ ] 19.1-04-PLAN.md -- Create sdk with stateful CipherBoxClient, events, bin, and share operations
- [ ] 19.1-05-PLAN.md -- Rewire web app hooks and stores to use SDK
- [ ] 19.1-06-PLAN.md -- Remove re-exports, update imports, configure Release Please

### Phase 20: Vault Migration

**Goal**: The server stores zero crypto material -- rootFolderKey lives in the IPFS vault blob, making the server a true zero-knowledge relay
**Depends on**: Phase 19 (IPNS must be reliable before making it a login-adjacent dependency)
**Requirements**: VAULT-01, VAULT-02, VAULT-03, VAULT-04, VAULT-05, VAULT-06
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

1. New users get vault blob v2 format on first login, with rootFolderKey ECIES-wrapped in the blob header and readable without any database round-trip
2. Existing users are lazily migrated to vault blob v2 on their next folder metadata publish, with the DB copy retained as a permanent fallback
3. The standalone recovery tool parses vault blob v2 and extracts rootFolderKey without needing the CipherBox API or database
4. The desktop app (Rust) parses vault blob v2 and uses the embedded rootFolderKey for FUSE mount initialization
5. The encryptedRootIpnsPrivateKey column is deprecated from the vaults table (HKDF derivation is the canonical path)
   **Plans**: TBD

### Phase 21: BYO-IPFS Node Support

**Goal**: Users can configure their own IPFS node for data sovereignty, with files pinned to both CipherBox and their personal node
**Depends on**: Phase 19 (stable IPNS resolution benefits BYO workflows)
**Requirements**: BYO-01, BYO-02, BYO-03, BYO-04, BYO-05, BYO-06, BYO-07
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

1. A user can enter their IPFS node endpoint and credentials in Settings, test the connection, and see a success/failure result
2. After configuring a BYO node, every file upload is pinned to both the CipherBox node (always) and the user's node (best-effort mirror)
3. All IPNS publishes still route through the CipherBox API regardless of BYO configuration (no bypass of optimistic concurrency)
4. BYO users see an advisory quota display (not enforced) with clear indication that storage is managed by their own node
5. The connection test endpoint validates reachability and API compatibility of the user's node before saving configuration
   **Plans**: TBD

### Phase 22: Performance Baselines Completion

**Goal**: Complete performance picture exists -- client-side timing, end-to-end journeys, load test results, and capacity recommendations are documented
**Depends on**: Phase 21 (all features must be stable to produce meaningful baselines)
**Requirements**: PERF-05, PERF-06, PERF-07, PERF-08
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

1. Client-side timing instrumentation captures encrypt/decrypt throughput, upload/download duration, and IPNS operation timing in the browser
2. End-to-end user journey timings are captured for login-to-vault, upload-to-visible, and share-to-accessible workflows
3. k6 load test scripts simulate concurrent users performing upload, download, publish, and resolve operations with documented pass/fail thresholds
4. Capacity thresholds are documented with scaling recommendations (max concurrent users, storage growth projections, IPNS publish throughput limits)
   **Plans**: TBD

## Progress

**Execution Order:**
Phases execute in numeric order: 18 -> 19 -> 19.1 -> 20 -> 21 -> 22

| Phase                              | Milestone | Plans Complete | Status      | Completed  |
| ---------------------------------- | --------- | -------------- | ----------- | ---------- |
| 18. Performance Instrumentation    | v1.1      | 2/2            | Complete    | 2026-03-07 |
| 19. IPNS Resolution Improvement    | v1.1      | 2/2            | Complete    | 2026-03-07 |
| 19.1 Extract Core Crypto SDK       | v1.1      | 6/6            | Complete    | 2026-03-20 |
| 20. Vault Migration                | v1.1      | 0/?            | Not started | -          |
| 21. BYO-IPFS Node Support          | v1.1      | 0/?            | Not started | -          |
| 22. Performance Baselines Complete | v1.1      | 0/?            | Not started | -          |

---

_Roadmap created: 2026-03-07_
_Last updated: 2026-03-20_

4. TEE republish batch duration histogram captures per-batch timing with success/failure labels

- **v1.0 Production** - Phases 11-17.1 (shipped 2026-03-05)
- **v1.1 IPFS Infrastructure** - Phases 18-22 (in progress)

**Goal**: Operators can observe IPFS/IPNS latency and API performance in Prometheus/Grafana before any architectural changes are made
**Depends on**: Nothing (first phase of milestone)
**Requirements**: PERF-01, PERF-02, PERF-03, PERF-04
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

1. Prometheus exposes duration histograms for IPNS resolve, IPNS publish, IPFS pin, and IPFS cat operations with per-operation labels
2. API endpoint response times are captured at p50/p95/p99 for all critical routes (auth, IPNS resolve/publish, file upload/download, folder CRUD)
3. Kubo node health metrics (peer count, bandwidth, datastore size) are visible in Prometheus via scraped Kubo endpoint
4. TEE republish batch duration histogram captures per-batch timing with success/failure labels

**Plans:** 2/2 plans complete

- [x] 18-02-PLAN.md -- Add Kubo scrape to Alloy, extend Grafana dashboard, create baseline benchmark script

**Depends on**: Phase 18 (baselines must exist to measure improvement)

2. IPNS resolution completes within 2 seconds in the normal case (DB-first with async DHT verification) and degrades gracefully to DB-only when DHT is slow
3. The standalone recovery tool resolves IPNS records via self-hosted Someguy without depending on the CipherBox API or delegated-ipfs.dev
4. No user-visible errors or stale metadata when the DHT is temporarily unreachable (DB fallback serves correct data)
   **Plans**: 2 plans

3. The standalone recovery tool parses vault blob v2 and extracts rootFolderKey without needing the CipherBox API or database
4. The desktop app (Rust) parses vault blob v2 and uses the embedded rootFolderKey for FUSE mount initialization
5. The encryptedRootIpnsPrivateKey column is deprecated from the vaults table (HKDF derivation is the canonical path)
   **Plans**: TBD

**Goal**: Users can configure their own IPFS node for data sovereignty, with files pinned to both CipherBox and their personal node
**Depends on**: Phase 19 (stable IPNS resolution benefits BYO workflows)
**Requirements**: BYO-01, BYO-02, BYO-03, BYO-04, BYO-05, BYO-06, BYO-07
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

2. After configuring a BYO node, every file upload is pinned to both the CipherBox node (always) and the user's node (best-effort mirror)
3. All IPNS publishes still route through the CipherBox API regardless of BYO configuration (no bypass of optimistic concurrency)
4. BYO users see an advisory quota display (not enforced) with clear indication that storage is managed by their own node
5. The connection test endpoint validates reachability and API compatibility of the user's node before saving configuration
   **Plans**: TBD

### Phase 22: Performance Baselines Completion

**Goal**: Complete performance picture exists -- client-side timing, end-to-end journeys, load test results, and capacity recommendations are documented
**Depends on**: Phase 21 (all features must be stable to produce meaningful baselines)
**Requirements**: PERF-05, PERF-06, PERF-07, PERF-08
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

2. End-to-end user journey timings are captured for login-to-vault, upload-to-visible, and share-to-accessible workflows
3. k6 load test scripts simulate concurrent users performing upload, download, publish, and resolve operations with documented pass/fail thresholds
4. Capacity thresholds are documented with scaling recommendations (max concurrent users, storage growth projections, IPNS publish throughput limits)
   **Plans**: TBD

The measurement difference accounts for some of the throughput gap, but the zero error rate is the significant improvement — Phase 18 had 18 timeouts under identical concurrency.

    81→
    82→## Key Observations
    83→
    84→1. **DHT warm-up matters significantly**: Staging someguy (8h uptime) is ~2x faster than local someguy (10min uptime). The accelerated DHT routing table fills over time, improving lookup speed.

   135→
   136→1. **Throughput plateaus at ~23-28 ops/s**: From 50→200 clients, throughput only grows from 22.86→28.50 ops/s. The staging VPS (4 vCPU, 8GB) is saturated — additional clients primarily increase latency.
   137→2. **The knee is at ~50 clients**: Throughput jumps from 12.14 (30 clients) to 22.86 (50 clients), then flattens. Kubo's pin concurrency maxes out around 50 parallel operations.
   138→3. **First errors at 200 clients**: 4 errors across 8,734 ops (0.05% error rate). 1 each in createFolder, moveItem, renameItem, uploadFile. Also 1 IPNS publish 409 conflict (expected concurrent sequence number collision). Error-free operation up to 100 clients.
   139→4. **uploadFile p99 reaches 21s at 200 clients**: p50 grows from 2.6s (10 clients) to 8.8s (200 clients). p99 goes from 4.7s to 21.0s — approaching typical HTTP timeout thresholds.
   140→5. **Kubo pin mean stays flat (~1.6s)**: Server-side pin latency doesn't degrade much with concurrency. The client-side latency increase is primarily queuing — more clients waiting for their turn.
   141→6. **Metadata-only operations degrade gracefully**: deleteItem/renameItem p50 grows from ~750ms (10 clients) to ~3.0s (200 clients).
   142→
   143→## Upload Flow Latency Breakdown (Prometheus Server-Side)
   144→
   145→Captured from staging `/metrics` endpoint after all load test runs (10–200 clients). Cumulative histograms.
   146→
   147→### Where uploadFile time goes
   148→
   149→A single SDK `uploadFile` call makes 5 sequential API calls:
   150→
   151→| Step | API Call                        | Server Mean | Role                             |
   152→| ---- | ------------------------------- | ----------- | -------------------------------- |
   153→| 1    | POST /ipfs/upload (ciphertext)  | **1.73s**   | Pin encrypted file to Kubo       |
   154→| 2    | POST /ipfs/upload (metadata)    | **1.73s**   | Pin encrypted file metadata      |
   155→| 3    | POST /ipns/publish-batch        | 0.11s       | DB upsert for file IPNS record   |
   156→| 4    | POST /ipfs/upload (folder meta) | **1.73s**   | Pin updated folder metadata      |
   157→| 5    | POST /ipns/publish              | 0.14s       | DB upsert for folder IPNS record |
   158→
   159→**Total server-side: ~5.4s** — aligns with the 5.1s p50 client-side at 100 clients.
   160→
   161→### Internal operation timing
   162→
   163→| Metric                          | Count   | Mean  | Notes                                               |
   164→| ------------------------------- | ------- | ----- | --------------------------------------------------- |
   165→| IPFS Pin (Kubo `pin add`)       | 172,387 | 1.56s | ~95% of upload endpoint time                        |
   166→| HTTP POST /ipfs/upload          | 172,387 | 1.64s | Pin + quota check + DB write                        |
   167→| IPNS Publish (DB upsert)        | 122,892 | 127ms | Fast — just a database write                        |
   168→| IPNS Publish Batch (DB upsert)  | 24,717  | 92ms  | Similar to single publish                           |
   169→| IPNS Publish (409 conflict)     | 1       | 4ms   | Expected at high concurrency (seq number collision) |
   170→| Async DHT propagation (success) | 147,285 | 838ms | Fire-and-forget, does not block client              |
   171→| Async DHT propagation (error)   | 324     | 17.2s | 0.22% error rate, does not affect client responses  |
   172→
   173→### Bottleneck analysis
   174→
   175→**Kubo IPFS pinning is the dominant bottleneck**, consuming ~95% of the upload endpoint latency. Each `uploadFile` requires 3 sequential pin operations (ciphertext, file metadata, folder metadata), totaling ~5s server-side at mean.
   176→
   177→IPNS publishing is negligible in the request path (DB upsert only, ~100-140ms). DHT propagation happens asynchronously and does not block the client.
   178→
   179→**Levers for improving upload performance:**
   180→
   181→- **Concurrent pins**: The 3 pin calls per upload are currently sequential. Pins 1+2 (ciphertext + file metadata) could be parallelized since they're independent.
   182→- **Kubo tuning**: Pin performance degrades under concurrent load — likely contention on Kubo's datastore. Investigate Kubo's `--pin-workers` setting or a faster datastore backend.
   183→- **Pin batching**: Multiple small metadata pins could potentially be coalesced.
   184→
   185→## Comparison Targets
   186→
   187→Phase 22 (Performance Baselines Completion) should:
   188→
   189→- Re-capture server-side Prometheus histograms for direct comparison with Phase 18 internal timings
   190→- Add client-side instrumentation for real user latency measurement
   191→- Document capacity limits and scaling recommendations
   192→- Performance regression threshold: >20% p95 increase requires investigation

1→# CipherBox - Claude AI Rules
     2→
     3→## Project Context
     4→
     5→CipherBox is a **technology demonstrator** for privacy-first encrypted cloud storage using IPFS/IPNS and Web3Auth. It is not a commercial product.
     6→
     7→## Documentation Structure
     8→
     9→| Document                                                     | Purpose                                    |
    10→| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------ |
    11→| `00-Preliminary-R&D/Documentation/PRD.md`                    | Product requirements, user journeys, scope |
    12→| `00-Preliminary-R&D/Documentation/TECHNICAL_ARCHITECTURE.md` | Encryption, key hierarchy, system design   |
    13→| `00-Preliminary-R&D/Documentation/API_SPECIFICATION.md`      | Backend endpoints, database schema         |
    14→| `00-Preliminary-R&D/Documentation/DATA_FLOWS.md`             | Sequence diagrams, test vectors            |
    15→| `00-Preliminary-R&D/Documentation/CLIENT_SPECIFICATION.md`   | Web UI, desktop app specs                  |
    16→| `00-Preliminary-R&D/Documentation/IMPLEMENTATION_ROADMAP.md` | Week-by-week development plan              |
    17→
    18→## Finalized Specifications
    19→
    20→**Current Version:** 1.11.1
    21→**Status:** Finalized (2026-01-20)
    22→
    23→### ⚠️ IMPORTANT: Do Not Edit Preliminary/Documentation Files
    24→
    25→All files in `00-Preliminary-R&D/Documentation/` are **FINALIZED** specifications (version 1.10.0, status: Finalized). These documents represent the agreed-upon design and should **NOT** be modified.
    26→**If you need to make changes:**
    27→
    28→- New implementation documentation should be created in a separate location
    29→- Working notes and updates belong in `.planning/` or project-specific directories
    30→- Do not modify version numbers or content in `00-Preliminary-R&D/Documentation/` unless explicityly authorized.
    31→
    32→## Terminology Standards
    33→
    34→Always use consistent terminology:
    35→
    36→| Correct                   | Avoid                                              |
    37→| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
    38→| `publicKey`               | `pubkey`, `user_pubkey`, `ownerPublicKey`          |
    39→| `privateKey`              | `privkey`, `user_private_key`                      |
    40→| `rootFolderKey`           | `rootKey`, `root_folder_key`                       |
    41→| `ipnsName`                | IPNS entry (for identifier)                        |
    42→| `ipnsRecord`              | IPNS entry (for data structure)                    |
    43→| `folderKey`               | `subfolderKey` (unless specifically for subfolder) |
    44→| `fileKey`                 | `file_key`                                         |
    45→| `keyEpoch`                | `epoch`, `key_epoch`                               |
    46→| `encryptedIpnsPrivateKey` | `encrypted_ipns_key`, `ipns_key_encrypted`         |
    47→| `teePublicKey`            | `tee_pubkey`, `TEE_public_key`                     |
    48→
    49→## Critical Security Rules
    50→
    51→1. **Never** suggest storing `privateKey` in localStorage/sessionStorage
    52→2. **Never** suggest logging sensitive keys
    53→3. **Never** suggest sending unencrypted keys to server
    54→4. **Always** use ECIES for key wrapping
    55→5. **Always** use AES-256-GCM for content encryption
    56→6. The server NEVER has access to plaintext or unencrypted keys
    57→7. **Always** encrypt `ipnsPrivateKey` with TEE public key before sending for republishing
    58→8. TEE decrypts IPNS keys in hardware only, signs, and immediately discards
    59→
    60→## API Development Workflow
    61→
    62→When working on `apps/api` code:
    63→
    64→1. **After modifying API endpoints, DTOs, or controllers**, regenerate the API client to keep the web app in sync:
    65→
    66→   ```bash
    67→   pnpm api:generate
    68→   ```
    69→
    70→   This command generates the OpenAPI spec from the API, regenerates the typed client in `@cipherbox/api-client`, builds the package, and runs lint fixes.
    71→
    72→2. **Always run `pnpm api:generate` before completing a feature** that touches the API to ensure type safety across the monorepo.
    73→
    74→3. **Commit the regenerated client files** (`packages/api-client/src/generated/` and `packages/api-client/src/models/`) along with your API changes.
    75→
    76→## Code Generation Guidelines
    77→
    78→When generating code for CipherBox:
    79→
    80→1. Use TypeScript for all JavaScript code
    81→2. Use `Uint8Array` for binary data, not strings
    82→3. Use Web Crypto API for browser encryption
    83→4. Use camelCase for API fields, snake_case for database columns
    84→5. Include proper error handling for crypto operations
    85→6. Clear sensitive data from memory after use
    86→
    87→## Architecture Decisions
    88→
    89→- **Auth:** Web3Auth for key derivation, CipherBox backend for tokens
    90→- **Storage:** IPFS via Kubo for files, IPNS for metadata (all relayed via CipherBox API)
    91→- **Encryption:** Client-side only, server is zero-knowledge
    92→- **Sync:** IPNS polling (30s interval), no push infrastructure
    93→- **Desktop:** FUSE mount for transparent file access
    94→- **TEE Republishing:** Phala Cloud (primary) / AWS Nitro (fallback) for automatic IPNS republishing every 3 hours
    95→- **Key Epochs:** TEE public keys rotate with 4-week grace period for seamless migration
    96→
    97→## Out of Scope (v1.0)
    98→
    99→Do not implement or suggest implementations for:
   100→
   101→- Billing/payments
   102→- File versioning
   103→- File/folder sharing
   104→- Mobile apps
   105→- Search/indexing
   106→- Collaborative editing
   107→- Team accounts
   108→
   109→## Verification with MCP Tools
   110→
   111→### Playwright MCP Verification (REQUIRED)
   112→
   113→**ALWAYS attempt to verify application changes using Playwright MCP** when it is available. This ensures implemented features work correctly at runtime.
   114→
   115→**When to use Playwright MCP:**
   116→
   117→- After implementing UI components
   118→- After modifying styles or layouts
   119→- After adding new pages or routes
   120→- After any user-facing changes
   121→- During GSD verification phase
   122→
   123→**Verification workflow:**
   124→
   125→```typescript
   126→// 1. Navigate to the app
   127→await mcp__playwright__navigate({ url: 'http://localhost:5173' });
   128→
   129→// 2. Wait for page to load
   130→await mcp__playwright__wait({ selector: '[data-testid="app-loaded"]' });
   131→
   132→// 3. Capture screenshot for visual verification
   133→await mcp__playwright__screenshot({ fullPage: true, name: 'verification' });
   134→
   135→// 4. Verify element existence
   136→const exists = await mcp__playwright__evaluate({
   137→  script: `!!document.querySelector('.expected-element')`,
   138→});
   139→
   140→// 5. Verify computed styles (for UI work)
   141→const styles = await mcp__playwright__evaluate({
   142→  script: `
   143→    const el = document.querySelector('.target');
   144→    const s = getComputedStyle(el);
   145→    return { backgroundColor: s.backgroundColor, color: s.color };
   146→  `,
   147→});
   148→
   149→// 6. Test interactions
   150→await mcp__playwright__click({ selector: 'button.action' });
   151→await mcp__playwright__wait({ selector: '.result-element' });
   152→```
   153→
   154→**If Playwright MCP is not available:**
   155→
   156→- Document what needs human verification
   157→- Provide manual test steps
   158→- Flag items in VERIFICATION.md
   159→
   160→### Pencil MCP for Design Work
   161→
   162→**When working on UI phases**, use Pencil MCP (if available) or parse `.pen` files directly to extract design specifications as the source of truth.
   163→
   164→**Design files location:** `designs/*.pen`
   165→
   166→**Verification against design:**
   167→
   168→1. Extract design specs from Pencil file
   169→2. Verify CSS values match exactly (hex codes, pixel values)
   170→3. Use Playwright MCP to verify computed styles at runtime
   171→4. Document any discrepancies with file/line references
   172→
   173→**Reference:** See `.claude/get-shit-done/references/pencil-design-workflow.md`
   174→
   175→## Git Workflow
   176→
   177→**Branch Protection Rules:**
   178→
   179→- **NEVER push directly to `main` branch** - all changes must go through feature branches and PRs
   180→- Create feature branches with descriptive names (e.g., `feat/add-auth`, `fix/ipns-publish`)
   181→- All commits should be made on feature branches first
   182→- Merge to main only via pull requests
   183→
   184→**Branch Naming:**
   185→
   186→- `feat/` - New features
   187→- `fix/` - Bug fixes
   188→- `docs/` - Documentation updates
   189→- `refactor/` - Code refactoring
   190→- `chore/` - Maintenance tasks
   191→
   192→**Commit Messages:**
   193→
   194→Commits must follow the [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) format. This is enforced by commitlint via a husky `commit-msg` hook.
   195→
   196→```text
   197→type(optional-scope): description
   198→
   199→[optional body]
   200→```
   201→
   202→Valid types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `perf`, `test`, `build`, `ci`, `chore`, `revert`. Any scope string is allowed (e.g., `feat(api): add health endpoint`).
   203→
   204→**Releases & Versioning:**
   205→
   206→- All packages share a single unified version (currently tracked in `.release-please-manifest.json`)
   207→- [Release Please](https://github.com/googleapis/release-please) automates changelog generation, version bumping, and GitHub Releases
   208→- On push to `main`, the `release-please.yml` workflow creates/updates a release PR with accumulated changes
   209→- When that PR is merged, Release Please creates a GitHub Release and `cipher-box-vX.Y.Z` tag (root package uses `include-component-in-tag: true` because release-please's multi-package release scanner cannot match bare `v{version}` tags to the root path)
   210→- Version bumps propagate to all `package.json` files, `Cargo.toml`, and `tauri.conf.json` via `release-please-config.json`
   211→- Staging deploys are triggered by pushing a tag matching `staging-v*` (e.g., `staging-v0.26.0-rc-1`). The `staging-` prefix avoids collision with release-please's `v{version}` tag pattern — previous `v*-staging*` format caused release-please to match staging pre-releases to the root package path, blocking tag creation. The `rc-N` suffix is a sequential counter allowing multiple staging deploys per version.
   212→

**Phase:** 19.2 - IPFS Upload Performance Optimization
**Confidence:** HIGH

### Key Findings

1. **The primary parallelization opportunity is between steps 2 and 3 of the upload flow.** The file IPNS batch publish and folder metadata update (pin + IPNS publish) have no data dependencies on each other. Running them concurrently with `Promise.allSettled` saves one full pin duration (~1.73s), reducing the 5-call sequence from ~5.4s to ~3.7s -- aligning with the success criteria target of ~3.5s at p50.

2. **Steps 1a and 1b (ciphertext pin + file metadata pin) CANNOT be parallelized** because the file metadata embeds the CID from the ciphertext pin. The baselines document incorrectly suggested pins 1+2 could be parallelized -- the actual dependency chain makes only steps 2+3 parallelizable.

3. **Kubo pebbleds is the recommended datastore alternative to flatfs** if per-pin latency needs further reduction. Badgerds is explicitly deprecated and scheduled for removal. PebbleDB (LSM-tree) has faster write throughput than flatfs, though at the cost of higher memory usage and read amplification. No published benchmarks exist for pebbleds vs flatfs v0.40.0, so empirical testing is needed.

4. **No new dependencies or API changes are needed.** The primary optimization (Lever 1) is a ~10-line change in `packages/sdk/src/client.ts` to wrap two sequential awaits in `Promise.allSettled`. The datastore optimization (Lever 2) is a Docker config change only.

1→# Roadmap: CipherBox v1.1 IPFS Infrastructure
     2→
     3→## Overview
     4→
     5→CipherBox v1.1 transforms the platform from "IPFS as a storage backend with database fallbacks" to "IPFS-native with the database serving only auth." The milestone establishes performance baselines before making changes, replaces the unreliable delegated-ipfs.dev dependency with self-hosted IPNS resolution, migrates rootFolderKey to an IPFS vault blob (achieving true zero-knowledge server), adds BYO-IPFS node support for data sovereignty, and completes performance baselines with client-side instrumentation and load testing after all features are stable.
     6→
     7→## Milestones
     8→
     9→- **v0.1 Staging MVP** - Phases 1-10 (shipped 2026-02-11)
    10→- **v1.0 Production** - Phases 11-17.1 (shipped 2026-03-05)
    11→- **v1.1 IPFS Infrastructure** - Phases 18-22 (in progress)
    12→
    13→## Phases
    14→
    15→**Phase Numbering:**
    16→
    17→- Integer phases (1, 2, 3): Planned milestone work
    18→- Decimal phases (2.1, 2.2): Urgent insertions (marked with INSERTED)
    19→
    20→Decimal phases appear between their surrounding integers in numeric order.
    21→
    22→- [x] **Phase 18: Performance Instrumentation** - Server-side Prometheus histograms and Kubo metrics scraping to establish baselines before any architectural changes (completed 2026-03-07)
    23→- [x] **Phase 19: IPNS Resolution Improvement** - Replace delegated-ipfs.dev with self-hosted Someguy sidecar for reliable IPNS routing, add latency histograms for resolve/publish operations (completed 2026-03-07)
    24→- [ ] **Phase 19.2: IPFS Upload Performance Optimization** - Optimize Kubo pinning path (concurrent pins, worker tuning, pin batching) to reduce upload latency (INSERTED)
    25→- [ ] **Phase 20: Vault Migration** - Move rootFolderKey to IPFS vault blob v2 format, making the server store zero crypto material
    26→- [ ] **Phase 21: BYO-IPFS Node Support** - User-configurable IPFS pinning endpoint with dual-pin strategy, Settings UI, and connection testing
    27→- [ ] **Phase 22: Performance Baselines Completion** - Client-side timing instrumentation, end-to-end journey timing, k6 load testing, and capacity documentation
    28→
    29→## Phase Details
    30→
    31→### Phase 18: Performance Instrumentation
    32→
    33→**Goal**: Operators can observe IPFS/IPNS latency and API performance in Prometheus/Grafana before any architectural changes are made
    34→**Depends on**: Nothing (first phase of milestone)
    35→**Requirements**: PERF-01, PERF-02, PERF-03, PERF-04
    36→**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):
    37→
    38→1. Prometheus exposes duration histograms for IPNS resolve, IPNS publish, IPFS pin, and IPFS cat operations with per-operation labels
    39→2. API endpoint response times are captured at p50/p95/p99 for all critical routes (auth, IPNS resolve/publish, file upload/download, folder CRUD)
    40→3. Kubo node health metrics (peer count, bandwidth, datastore size) are visible in Prometheus via scraped Kubo endpoint
    41→4. TEE republish batch duration histogram captures per-batch timing with success/failure labels

    48→- [x] 18-02-PLAN.md -- Add Kubo scrape to Alloy, extend Grafana dashboard, create baseline benchmark script
    49→
    50→### Phase 19: IPNS Resolution Improvement
    51→
    52→**Goal**: Users experience reliable, fast IPNS resolution without dependency on external delegated-ipfs.dev service
    53→**Depends on**: Phase 18 (baselines must exist to measure improvement)
    54→**Requirements**: IPNS-01, IPNS-02, IPNS-03, IPNS-04
    55→**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):
    56→
    57→1. Self-hosted Someguy is deployed alongside Kubo and serves as the IPNS routing provider, with delegated-ipfs.dev fully removed from the resolution path

1→# Phase 19.2: IPFS Upload Performance Optimization - Research
     2→
     3→**Researched:** 2026-03-23
     4→**Domain:** IPFS Kubo pinning performance, NestJS API concurrency, Docker infrastructure tuning
     5→**Confidence:** HIGH
     6→
     7→## Summary
     8→
     9→The upload bottleneck is well-understood from Phase 19 baselines: each `uploadFile` SDK call makes 5 sequential API calls, 3 of which are `POST /ipfs/upload` (pin operations). Each pin takes ~1.73s mean, totaling ~5.4s server-side per upload. Kubo IPFS pinning consumes ~95% of the upload endpoint latency. IPNS publishing is negligible (~100-140ms, DB upsert only).
    10→
    11→There are three independent optimization levers, ordered by expected impact and implementation complexity. Lever 1 (concurrent pins at the SDK/API orchestration level) is the highest-impact, lowest-risk change since it requires no Kubo configuration changes. Lever 2 (Kubo datastore backend swap from flatfs to pebbleds) targets per-pin latency but requires Docker volume recreation and data migration. Lever 3 (multi-file batch add to Kubo in a single HTTP request) is the most complex but could eliminate per-request overhead for metadata pins.
    12→
    13→**Primary recommendation:** Implement concurrent pin orchestration in the SDK client first (Lever 1), then benchmark. If further improvement is needed, swap the Kubo datastore to pebbleds (Lever 2). Only pursue batch add (Lever 3) if the first two are insufficient.
    14→
    15→<phase_requirements>
    16→
    17→## Phase Requirements
    18→
    19→| ID      | Description                                                                                                 | Research Support                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
    20→| ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
    21→| PERF-09 | IPFS Upload Performance Optimization -- Upload operations measurably faster by optimizing Kubo pinning path | All three optimization levers (concurrent pins, datastore tuning, batch add) directly address this. Load test infrastructure exists for before/after comparison. Prometheus histograms already capture per-operation timing. |
    22→

    24→
    25→## Standard Stack
    26→
    27→### Core (Already in Project)
    28→
    29→| Library             | Version   | Purpose                               | Why Standard                                                                     |
    30→| ------------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
    31→| Kubo                | v0.40.0   | IPFS node (pinning, content storage)  | Already deployed, v0.40.0 has flatfs rewrite with atomic batch ops               |
    32→| NestJS              | (current) | API framework                         | Already in use, supports async/await concurrency natively                        |
    33→| @cipherbox/sdk      | workspace | Stateful client orchestrating uploads | Already built in Phase 19.1, this is the code that sequences the 5 API calls     |
    34→| @cipherbox/sdk-core | workspace | Stateless upload/IPFS/IPNS functions  | Already built, `uploadFile` and `updateFolderMetadataAndPublish` are the targets |
    35→| vitest              | ^3.0.5    | Load test runner                      | Already used in `tests/load/`                                                    |
    36→| prom-client         | (current) | Prometheus metrics                    | Already instrumented with `cipherbox_ipfs_ipns_duration_seconds`                 |
    37→
    38→### Supporting (No New Dependencies Needed)
    39→
    40→This phase requires no new libraries. All changes are orchestration-level (Promise.all), Docker config changes, and potentially Kubo CLI commands for datastore migration.
    41→
    42→## Architecture Patterns
    43→
    44→### Current Upload Flow (5 Sequential API Calls)
    45→
    46→```
    47→SDK client.uploadFile()
    48→  |
    49→  v
    50→1. sdkCore.uploadFile()
    51→   |-> addToIpfs(ciphertext)         -> POST /ipfs/upload  -> Kubo api/v0/add  [~1.73s]
    52→   |-> createFileMetadata()
    53→       |-> addToIpfs(encryptedMeta)  -> POST /ipfs/upload  -> Kubo api/v0/add  [~1.73s]
    54→  |
    55→  v
    56→2. sdkCore.batchPublishIpnsRecords() -> POST /ipns/publish-batch              [~0.11s]
    57→  |
    58→  v
    59→3. sdkCore.updateFolderMetadataAndPublish()
    60→   |-> addToIpfs(folderMeta)         -> POST /ipfs/upload  -> Kubo api/v0/add  [~1.73s]
    61→   |-> createAndPublishIpnsRecord()  -> POST /ipns/publish                     [~0.14s]
    62→                                                              Total: ~5.44s
    63→```
    64→
    65→### Dependency Analysis of the 5 Calls
    66→
    67→| Step | Operation                  | Depends On                                                    | Independent?        |
    68→| ---- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
    69→| 1a   | Pin ciphertext             | Nothing                                                       | YES                 |
    70→| 1b   | Pin file metadata          | Needs CID from step 1a (cid is embedded in FileMetadata)      | NO -- depends on 1a |
    71→| 2    | Publish file IPNS record   | Needs metadata CID from step 1b                               | Sequential after 1b |
    72→| 3a   | Pin folder metadata        | Needs FilePointer (which needs fileMetaIpnsName from step 1b) | Sequential after 1b |
    73→| 3b   | Publish folder IPNS record | Needs CID from step 3a                                        | Sequential after 3a |
    74→
    75→**Key insight:** Steps 1a and 1b are NOT independent -- the file metadata contains the CID from step 1a. However, steps 2 and 3a ARE partially independent: the IPNS batch publish (step 2) and the folder metadata pin (step 3a) could execute concurrently since they don't depend on each other's results.
    76→
    77→### Revised Understanding of Parallelization Opportunity
    78→
    79→Looking more carefully at the code:
    80→
    81→1. `sdkCore.uploadFile()` (steps 1a + 1b) -- sequential, CID dependency
    82→2. `sdkCore.batchPublishIpnsRecords()` (step 2) -- needs fileMetaIpnsName from step 1b
    83→3. `sdkCore.updateFolderMetadataAndPublish()` (steps 3a + 3b) -- needs FilePointer from step 1b
    84→
    85→Steps 2 and 3 are currently sequential in `client.uploadFile()` (lines 612-621 of client.ts). They CAN be parallelized:
    86→
    87→```typescript
    88→// Current (sequential):
    89→await sdkCore.batchPublishIpnsRecords([uploadResult.ipnsRecord], this.ctx);
    90→const { newSequenceNumber } = await sdkCore.updateFolderMetadataAndPublish({...});
    91→
    92→// Optimized (concurrent):
    93→const [_, { newSequenceNumber }] = await Promise.all([
    94→  sdkCore.batchPublishIpnsRecords([uploadResult.ipnsRecord], this.ctx),
    95→  sdkCore.updateFolderMetadataAndPublish({...}),
    96→]);
    97→```
    98→
    99→This saves one pin duration (~1.73s) because `updateFolderMetadataAndPublish` internally does a pin + IPNS publish, and we overlap it with the IPNS batch publish.
   100→
   101→**Expected savings:** ~1.73s (one pin) off the total ~5.44s = ~3.71s target, which aligns with the success criteria target of ~3.5s at p50.
   102→
   103→### Pattern 1: Concurrent Pin + IPNS Publish at SDK Level
   104→
   105→**What:** Parallelize the file IPNS batch publish and folder metadata update in `CipherBoxClient.uploadFile()`.
   106→
   107→**When to use:** Always -- these two operations have no data dependencies between them.
   108→
   109→**Implementation location:** `packages/sdk/src/client.ts`, `uploadFile()` method, lines 611-621.
   110→
   111→```typescript
   112→// In CipherBoxClient.uploadFile():
   113→// BEFORE: sequential
   114→await sdkCore.batchPublishIpnsRecords([uploadResult.ipnsRecord], this.ctx);
   115→const { newSequenceNumber } = await sdkCore.updateFolderMetadataAndPublish({...});
   116→
   117→// AFTER: concurrent
   118→const [, publishResult] = await Promise.all([
   119→  sdkCore.batchPublishIpnsRecords([uploadResult.ipnsRecord], this.ctx),
   120→  sdkCore.updateFolderMetadataAndPublish({
   121→    children: updatedChildren,
   122→    folderKey: folder.folderKey,
   123→    ipnsPrivateKey: folder.ipnsKeypair.privateKey,
   124→    ipnsName: folderIpnsName,
   125→    sequenceNumber: folder.sequenceNumber,
   126→    ctx: this.ctx,
   127→  }),
   128→]);
   129→const { newSequenceNumber } = publishResult;
   130→```
   131→
   132→### Pattern 2: Kubo Datastore Backend Swap (flatfs -> pebbleds)
   133→
   134→**What:** Replace the default flatfs block storage with pebbleds (PebbleDB) for faster write throughput.
   135→
   136→**When to use:** When per-pin latency is the bottleneck and concurrent load causes filesystem contention.
   137→
   138→**Why pebbleds:** LSM-tree based datastores like Pebble have very fast write performance (blocks streamed to disk) compared to flatfs (one file per block, filesystem metadata overhead). Pebble is the modern replacement for deprecated badgerds. Badgerds is explicitly deprecated in Kubo and will be removed.
   139→
   140→**Trade-offs:**
   141→
   142→- Pebbleds uses more memory than flatfs
   143→- Read amplification for lookups (blocks need index lookup)
   144→- Requires Docker volume recreation (cannot convert in-place)
   145→
   146→**Implementation:** Requires Docker compose changes + Kubo init with `--profile pebbleds`.
   147→
   148→### Pattern 3: Multi-File Batch Add via Kubo API
   149→
   150→**What:** Send multiple files in a single `POST /api/v0/add` request using multipart form-data, reducing per-request overhead.
   151→
   152→**When to use:** When multiple small metadata blobs need pinning (file metadata + folder metadata are both small JSON).
   153→
   154→**Implementation complexity:** HIGH -- requires changes to the `LocalProvider.pinFile()` interface to support batching, plus a new `pinFiles()` method or endpoint.
   155→
   156→### Anti-Patterns to Avoid
   157→
   158→- **Don't batch the ciphertext pin with metadata pins:** The ciphertext pin is large (user file data). Batching it with small metadata would not help and could increase memory pressure. Keep large files as individual pins.
   159→- **Don't add a new batch pin API endpoint:** The existing upload endpoint already does pin + quota tracking atomically. Adding a batch endpoint would complicate quota accounting and error rollback. Instead, parallelize at the SDK orchestration level.
   160→- **Don't switch to badgerds:** It's explicitly deprecated and scheduled for removal from Kubo. Use pebbleds if changing datastores.
   161→- **Don't modify the `addToIpfs` → `POST /ipfs/upload` contract for batching:** The quota tracking per-pin in the API controller makes batching at the API level complex. Parallelization at the SDK level is cleaner.
   162→
   163→## Don't Hand-Roll
   164→
   165→| Problem                 | Don't Build                     | Use Instead                                   | Why                                                                                               |
   166→| ----------------------- | ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
   167→| Kubo pin queuing        | Custom job queue for pins       | Promise.all at SDK level                      | Kubo handles its own internal concurrency; we just need to avoid serializing independent requests |
   168→| Datastore migration     | Manual block-by-block migration | `ipfs init --profile pebbleds` + fresh volume | Kubo handles datastore initialization; manual migration is error-prone                            |
   169→| Pin latency measurement | Custom timing in API controller | Existing Prometheus histograms                | `cipherbox_ipfs_ipns_duration_seconds` with `operation=pin` already captures this                 |
   170→| Load test comparison    | Manual before/after spreadsheet | Existing `tests/load/` metrics collector      | JSON reports with percentiles already generated                                                   |
   171→
   172→## Common Pitfalls
   173→
   174→### Pitfall 1: Promise.all Error Handling in Upload
   175→
   176→**What goes wrong:** If the file IPNS publish fails and the folder metadata publish succeeds (or vice versa) in the Promise.all, the system is in an inconsistent state.
   177→**Why it happens:** Promise.all rejects on first failure, leaving the other promise's side effects in an unknown state.
   178→**How to avoid:** Use Promise.allSettled instead of Promise.all, then check both results. If either fails, the upload should fail entirely (the existing retry/conflict logic handles this for IPNS publishes).
   179→**Warning signs:** Partial upload state -- file IPNS record exists but folder doesn't reference it, or folder references a file whose IPNS record doesn't exist yet.
   180→
   181→### Pitfall 2: Kubo Concurrent Pin Contention at High Load
   182→
   183→**What goes wrong:** Under high concurrency (50+ clients), parallel pins from multiple uploads compete for Kubo's datastore write lock, potentially increasing per-pin latency rather than decreasing it.
   184→**Why it happens:** Flatfs writes one file per block, and filesystem metadata operations (create, fsync) serialize under the OS. Even with concurrent HTTP requests, Kubo serializes writes internally.
   185→**How to avoid:** Benchmark before and after on the actual deployment. If per-pin latency increases under parallel pins, the net effect may be neutral. The pebbleds datastore handles concurrent writes better due to LSM-tree batching.
   186→**Warning signs:** Pin p50 increasing while total upload time stays the same or gets worse.
   187→
   188→### Pitfall 3: Docker Volume Migration for Datastore Change
   189→
   190→**What goes wrong:** Changing Kubo's datastore backend requires a fresh IPFS repo. Existing pinned data is lost.
   191→**Why it happens:** Kubo datastores are not interchangeable; each has a different on-disk format.
   192→**How to avoid:** For the local dev/test infrastructure, this is acceptable -- the data is ephemeral test data. For staging, the user will manually redeploy the docker stack (as stated in the phase context). Document the migration steps clearly.
   193→**Warning signs:** Kubo fails to start after config change because the existing volume has flatfs data.
   194→
   195→### Pitfall 4: IPFS_PROFILE=server Overriding Datastore Config
   196→
   197→**What goes wrong:** The staging docker-compose sets `IPFS_PROFILE: server` which may override manual datastore configuration.
   198→**Why it happens:** Kubo profiles are applied at init time and configure multiple settings including the datastore.
   199→**How to avoid:** When switching to pebbleds, use `IPFS_PROFILE: server,pebbleds` (comma-separated profiles) or apply pebbleds after server profile. Verify the resulting config with `ipfs config Datastore.Spec`.
   200→**Warning signs:** After setting pebbleds, `ipfs config show` still shows flatfs.
   201→
   202→### Pitfall 5: Measuring the Wrong Thing
   203→
   204→**What goes wrong:** Client-side latency improvements don't match server-side improvements because the load test SDK overhead or network latency masks the savings.
   205→**Why it happens:** The load test measures end-to-end SDK operation time, which includes HTTP overhead, JSON serialization, and client-side crypto.
   206→**How to avoid:** Use BOTH Prometheus server-side histograms (pin duration, endpoint duration) AND the load test client-side metrics. Compare both before/after.
   207→**Warning signs:** Server-side pin p50 drops but load test uploadFile p50 doesn't change.
   208→
   209→## Code Examples
   210→
   211→### Example 1: Current uploadFile in SDK client (to be modified)
   212→
   213→```typescript
   214→// Source: packages/sdk/src/client.ts lines 589-660
   215→// Current sequential flow:
   216→const uploadResult = await sdkCore.uploadFile({...});
   217→
   218→// Step 2: File IPNS publish
   219→await sdkCore.batchPublishIpnsRecords([uploadResult.ipnsRecord], this.ctx);
   220→
   221→// Step 3: Folder metadata update (includes pin + IPNS publish)

   224→
   225→### Example 2: Parallelized version
   226→

   228→// Steps 2 and 3 in parallel:
   229→const [batchResult, folderResult] = await Promise.allSettled([
   230→  sdkCore.batchPublishIpnsRecords([uploadResult.ipnsRecord], this.ctx),
   231→  sdkCore.updateFolderMetadataAndPublish({
   232→    children: updatedChildren,
   233→    folderKey: folder.folderKey,
   234→    ipnsPrivateKey: folder.ipnsKeypair.privateKey,
   235→    ipnsName: folderIpnsName,
   236→    sequenceNumber: folder.sequenceNumber,
   237→    ctx: this.ctx,
   238→  }),
   239→]);
   240→
   241→// Check results
   242→if (folderResult.status === 'rejected') throw folderResult.reason;
   243→if (batchResult.status === 'rejected') {
   244→  // File IPNS publish failed but folder metadata is already updated.
   245→  // Log warning but don't fail -- the file IPNS record will be created
   246→  // on next publish attempt. The FilePointer in folder metadata is valid.
   247→  console.warn('[SDK] File IPNS batch publish failed:', batchResult.reason);
   248→}
   249→const { newSequenceNumber } = folderResult.value;
   250→```
